examples.label: Transfer demo zone zonetransfer.me (public test target)
Find NS records then attempt transfer
examples.command:
dig ns inlanefreight.com
dig axfr @ns1.inlanefreight.com inlanefreight.com

notes: AXFR (`dig axfr <domain> @<ns>`) dumps the entire zone if the NS is misconfigured - instant full subdomain/host list. Rare but devastating; always try it against every NS record before brute forcing. Zone transfers (AXFR) are only allowed when the nameserver is misconfigured. A successful transfer dumps all DNS records including internal hostnames, IPs, and subdomains. Test with 'dig axfr' against each NS record. Also covered in: CPTS Ch05 (Information Gathering – Web Edition).

name: DNS - Zone Transfer (AXFR)
description: A misconfigured name server that allows AXFR hands you every record in the zone. zonetransfer.me is a public practice target.

defense.why_it_works: A DNS zone transfer (AXFR) is a replication mechanism for secondary nameservers. Misconfigured DNS servers that allow transfers from arbitrary sources expose the entire zone in a single response: all subdomains, IP mappings, internal hostnames, mail infrastructure, and reverse-lookup records.
defense.prerequisites: A target domain and an authoritative name server misconfigured to allow AXFR from arbitrary hosts.
defense.impact: A successful transfer dumps the entire DNS zone at once — every subdomain, internal hostname, and IP mapping — instantly mapping the full external (and sometimes internal) footprint.
defense.detection:
Zone transfer requests (AXFR/IXFR) from arbitrary external sources are abnormal — virtually no legitimate client should issue an AXFR against a public nameserver. These requests are visible in DNS server logs and can trigger IDS/SIEM alerts. While most servers are configured to prevent unauthorised zone transfers, a successful attempt indicates a critical misconfiguration.

[MITRE T1590.002 M1056] Monitor for suspicious queries to DNS infrastructure. AXFR queries from untrusted source IPs are a high-confidence indicator of reconnaissance activity.
defense.artifacts: The AXFR request is recorded in the DNS server's query log with the source IP, and is anomalous — virtually no legitimate client issues AXFR against a public server.
defense.prevention:
Configure authoritative nameservers to restrict AXFR/IXFR responses to explicitly authorized secondary server IPs using ACLs (e.g., BIND `allow-transfer` directive; PowerDNS `allow-axfr-ips`). Audit DNS server configurations regularly and alert on zone transfer attempts from unexpected sources.

[MITRE T1590.002 M1056] Server-side ACLs are highly effective at preventing unauthorized zone transfers and should be configured on all authoritative nameservers.
defense.evasion: Attempt AXFR against every one of the domain's nameservers, not just the primary - secondary/legacy nameservers are more often left misconfigured to allow transfers. There is otherwise little to evade: a single AXFR request either succeeds or is refused, and any attempt from an unlisted source is logged as anomalous.
defense.misconfiguration: DNS zone transfers (AXFR queries) are permitted to any requesting host — not restricted to authorized secondary DNS servers. This exposes the entire DNS zone (all hostnames, IPs, mail servers, internal naming conventions) to any attacker who can reach the DNS port. Even without AXFR, DNS servers that respond to ANY queries or provide detailed error messages leak zone structure.
